title: Your harness is weighing you down!
html:
Your harness is weighing you down!

Coding agents are transforming software engineering and other computational fields. They reshape how human work with language models and how models act on behave of humans in the world. Models provide the core intelligence behind these agents, while harnesses—the systems around the models—are increasingly seen as essential to putting that intelligence to work.

Harnesses control how models use tools, manage context, and work through tasks on behalf of users. Popular examples include Claude Code, Codex CLI, Cursor, Pi, and OpenCode. Research shows that harness techniques can improve model performance and reliability on coding tasks. Yet recommendations about which harness to use often rely on personal preference and word of mouth. We still lack a systematic understanding of how harnesses compare across models and how harness choice affects what a model can solve.

This gap makes it difficult to choose the right model–harness combination. Each time we open a coding agent, we implicitly choose a harness, even if we focus only on selecting a model. If harness choice substantially affects task success or cost, evaluating a model in a single harness gives an incomplete picture of its performance. If the effect is small, we need to understand what choosing a different harness actually buys us.

To close the gap in understanding harness and model performance jointly, we measure task success and cost for seven models and three harnesses—Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Pi—on SWE-bench Lite and Terminal-Bench 2. We randomly sample 30 tasks per benchmark and run each evaluated model–harness pair three times per task, for 2,340 rollouts in total. A rollout is one attempt at one task.

Our study reveals three key findings:

  1. Harness choice affects cost more than task success on the benchmarks we test.
  2. More complex harnesses do not always deliver better results. Simpler harnesses such as Pi can be highly efficient.
  3. Models can perform competitively outside their provider’s harness.

We breakdown each findings in detail below.

(1/3) The harness effects cost, not correctness.

At fixed model, Claude Code runs at about 2.0× Pi's and 3.1× Codex's geometric-mean cost on SWE-bench, and about 2.1× Pi's on Terminal-Bench, while the harness offsets on success stay within ±3 points. That is the strongest form yet of "the harness moves cost, not correctness".

  • The open-source harness wins on cost at no detectable loss in accuracy. pi holds 6 of the 7 frontier positions across the two benchmarks; Claude Code holds none. The heavier harnesses were not more efficient: on both benchmarks, pi used fewer tokens than the maker's harness for every model.

  • A model does not need its maker's harness. Claude models outside Claude Code, and GPT models outside Codex, lost no accuracy we could detect; the maker's harness cost more in 12 of 12 cases.

Figure 1 plots the 13 systems on each benchmark: cost per rollout on the x-axis, resolved rate on the y-axis (the share of rollouts that passed the task's tests). The stepped line is the Pareto frontier: the systems no other system beats on both cost and accuracy. In panel (a), the filled red square and the faint hollow red diamond are the same model, Fable 5, at the same height but at two different costs.

Figure 1. The frontier runs through pi squares on both benchmarks and one Codex triangle on SWE-bench; no Claude Code diamond is on it. Each marker is the mean of 90 rollouts, with tokens priced on one frozen public rate card so every system is billed the same way.

How we measured

The models were Claude Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.8 and Fable 5; GPT-5.6 Luna and Sol; and Kimi K3. Claude models ran in Claude Code and pi, GPT models in Codex CLI and pi, and Kimi K3 in pi only: 13 systems per benchmark. Every system got the same 30 tasks, task prompt, Docker images and graders, with reasoning effort "high" wherever the model exposes it. Each harness keeps its own system prompt and tools; that is what we test. The basic comparison is one model on one task in each of two harnesses.

Cost is token usage priced on one public price list (direct-API prices as of 2026-09-01), so subscription, cloud and API runs are priced alike; the dollar figures are list prices, not invoices. We averaged the three runs within each task and drew 95% intervals by resampling the 30 tasks. SWE-bench comparisons are corrected for testing several models at once, except the Opus pair and the two Codex pairs, whose runs came from different batches or billing routes and are reported without a formal test. So are all Terminal-Bench comparisons, because the Claude Code runs happened after the pi and Codex runs.

The harness moves the bill, not the answer

Figure 2 compares each maker's harness with pi for the six models that ran in both: on the left, the accuracy difference with its 95% interval and a "same" line at zero; on the right, how many times more the maker's harness cost, on a log scale. Every left-hand interval reaches or crosses zero, and every right-hand marker sits right of "same". Hollow markers in panel (a) are the three pairs reported without a formal test.

Figure 2. In all 12 comparisons the accuracy interval includes zero. The maker's harness cost 1.1 to 2.1 times pi's mean spend on SWE-bench and 1.2 to 2.0 times on Terminal-Bench, and cost more on 20 to 29 of the 30 tasks in every pair.

The cleanest case is Fable 5 on SWE-bench Lite. In both harnesses it solved 86 of 90 rollouts, with the same outcome on 28 of 30 tasks. The accuracy difference is 0.0 percentage points (95% interval −3.3 to +3.3). Claude Code cost $0.87 per rollout against pi's $0.42, and cost more on 29 of 30 tasks. The other SWE-bench differences run from −5.6 points (Sonnet) to +7.8 (Haiku). For scale, swapping Haiku for Opus inside one harness moved accuracy by 24 to 28 points. Of the 12 cost multiples, 11 have intervals that exclude 1×; Sonnet's on SWE-bench reaches down to 0.99×.

The gap is input tokens. With Fable, both harnesses made about 12 model calls per rollout, but Claude Code sent 25.5k prompt tokens per call against pi's 8.6k. Across the four Claude models, Claude Code adds a roughly constant 14k to 17k tokens to every call: the system prompt, the tool definitions and the conversation so far. Cached tokens are billed at a tenth of the price, so the cost multiple for Fable, 2.1×, sits below its token multiple, 3×. In other words, the harness adds a roughly fixed fee to every call.

The model shapes the cost curve; the harness stretches it

Figure 3 sorts each system's 90 rollouts from cheapest to most expensive and plots the running share solved (y) against the running cost per rollout (x). Each curve ends at its system's point from Figure 1. Compare two curves of the same colour: the maker's-harness curve is the pi curve stretched to the right.

Figure 3. On SWE-bench, Luna reaches its final rate within about $0.02 per rollout and Fable, Sol and Opus in pi by about $0.2 to $0.4, while Haiku and Sonnet keep spending to $0.6 to $0.9 with little added success. Systems drawn in full colour led the frontier at some level of spend.

At equal spend, the pi curve sits above the maker's-harness curve for more than 99% of the spend range they share, for 5 of 6 models on SWE-bench and all 6 on Terminal-Bench. The exception is Haiku on SWE-bench, where the two curves cross back and forth. Fable reaches half of its final successes by $0.11 per rollout in pi and by $0.22 in Claude Code, and both end at 96%. In other words, choose the model for the cost curve you want; in these six pairs the harness moved the end of the curve, not its shape.

The thin harness is the cheaper way to run every model

The SWE-bench frontier is Luna (in pi and in Codex), then Opus, Sol and Fable in pi; the Terminal-Bench frontier is Luna and Sol in pi. pi is a minimal open-source coding agent with four tools: read, bash, edit and write. It also ran the highest-scoring system on each benchmark: Fable at 96% on SWE-bench, tied with Claude Code, and Sol at 83% on Terminal-Bench. This follows from the first finding: pi ran each model at accuracy we could not tell apart, for less money, so no maker's harness can sit on the cost frontier. Membership is on the means; in task resamples the top three pi systems keep their places 85% to 99% of the time, and Claude Code with Fable, tied on accuracy, reaches the frontier 31% of the time.

The heavier harnesses were not more efficient. Figure 4 sets price aside: each of its six panels plots final task success (y) against one measured resource per rollout (x) for the 13 SWE-bench systems (9 in the wall-clock panel). In the first panel, the filled red square at top left, Fable in pi, is the only marker on the token frontier; the faint red diamond beside it is Fable in Claude Code.

Figure 4. Across the 13 systems, token use tracks the model: systems that used fewer tokens solved more tasks (rank correlation −0.82, p = 0.0011), and within each model pi used fewer tokens than the maker's harness (6 of 6). The step and tool-event panels are for orientation only, because each harness counts a step differently.

On SWE-bench, pi used fewer tokens than the maker's harness for 6 of 6 models, from 1.2× fewer (Haiku, Sonnet) to 3.0× fewer (Fable: 106k tokens per rollout against 319k). Claude Code logged 14% to 25% fewer steps for Haiku and Sonnet, but every step carried the added tokens, so Haiku's bill still rose 1.4×. The same holds on Terminal-Bench, where pi used fewer tokens than the maker's harness for all six models.

Token use tracks the model far more than the harness. Haiku in pi used 2.5M tokens per rollout, 23× what Fable in pi used, and 6.3× as many steps (75 against 12), and solved 51% of its rollouts. In other words, the efficient system is a strong model in a thin harness. Putting a weak model in a heavier harness raised its bill without a detectable lift in accuracy.

A model does not need its maker's harness

Claude Code and Codex come from the model makers, so their own models might be expected to do best in them. If so, the maker's-harness markers in Figure 2 would sit right of zero with intervals that do not touch it. They do not. Of the 12 comparisons, 4 favour the maker's harness, 7 favour pi and 1 is an exact tie, and every interval includes zero.

Combining the four Claude models (120 task pairs), Claude Code scored +2.2 percentage points against pi on SWE-bench (−1.4 to +5.8) and −2.2 on Terminal-Bench (−6.1 to +1.7). Combining the two GPT models (60 task pairs), Codex scored −1.1 against pi on SWE-bench (−6.1 to +3.9) and −5.0 on Terminal-Bench (−11.7 to +0.6). Pooled over all six Terminal-Bench pairs the maker's harness is at −3.1 (−6.7 to 0.0), so if anything the sign there runs against it. The maker's harness cost more in 12 of 12 pairs, from 1.15× (Luna in Codex) to 2.1× (Opus in Claude Code). In other words, a Claude model outside Claude Code, or a GPT model outside Codex, lost no accuracy we could detect, and cost less.

What this does not show

With 30 tasks per benchmark, the 95% interval around a same-model difference is up to about ±11 points. A real harness effect of a few points would slip through; more tasks would narrow it. The strongest hint of one is Haiku on SWE-bench, +7.8 points with an interval that starts at zero, but on Terminal-Bench the sign reverses (−6.7). SWE-bench Lite is easy for Fable, which solved 96%; Haiku and Sonnet, which solved 51% to 64%, show the same pattern with wider intervals.

On Terminal-Bench, the Claude Code runs happened after the pi and Codex runs, and only Claude Code ran under a 100-turn ceiling, which 4 of its Haiku rollouts hit without solving the task; 81 of 1,170 rollouts also hit task time limits and count as failures. Rerunning all three harnesses in one window under one turn rule would remove the first two problems. Frontier positions across vendors depend on the price list: Luna's $0.20 per million input tokens anchors the cheap end of both frontiers, and a repricing would move points but not the same-model comparisons.

Every harness ran headless (no interactive terminal). Permission prompts, IDE integration, memory, sub-agents, web search, MCP servers (external tool plug-ins) and skills were never exercised, and a harness may earn its cost on workloads that use them. We do not claim that harness choice never affects correctness, only that on these two benchmarks, with reasoning effort matched, we could not detect an effect.

In short

Across 12 same-model comparisons on two benchmarks, swapping the harness produced no detectable change in accuracy, while the maker's harness cost 1.1 to 2.1 times as much per rollout. The open-source harness held 6 of 7 frontier positions and used fewer tokens than the maker's harness for every model. No model did detectably better in its maker's harness. Every chart and per-task breakdown is on the dashboard at https://agentbrane-dashboard.pages.dev/.
